nameStory: Alpine sorrel gets its name from two key features: 'alpine' refers to its high-elevation mountain habitat, while 'sorrel' comes from the Old French 'surele,' meaning sour. The leaves have a distinctly tangy, lemony taste that's been enjoyed by mountain climbers and indigenous peoples for centuries as a refreshing trail snack.
description: Alpine sorrel is a small, hardy perennial herb that hugs the ground in New England's highest peaks. This compact plant rarely grows taller than 8 inches, forming low clumps of kidney-shaped leaves that emerge directly from the base. Its tiny reddish flowers cluster on slender stalks above the foliage, creating delicate spikes that dance in mountain breezes. This arctic survivor is perfectly adapted to harsh alpine conditions where few other plants can thrive.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Distinctive kidney or heart-shaped leaves with a sour, lemony taste when chewed. The leaves feel succulent and slightly waxy, growing 1-3 inches wide on long stalks directly from the ground.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny greenish-red flowers arranged in narrow, spike-like clusters on stems that rise above the leaves. Individual flowers are barely noticeable but create colorful displays en masse.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, cushion-like clumps that hug the ground, rarely exceeding 8 inches tall. All leaves emerge from the base with no obvious central stem.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, papery winged fruits that turn bright red or pink, often more conspicuous than the flowers. These heart-shaped seeds have thin, translucent wings.

habitat: In New England, alpine sorrel clings to life in the harshest mountain environments above treeline, particularly on Mount Washington and other White Mountain peaks. Look for it in rocky crevices, gravelly slopes, and alpine meadows where snow lingers late into summer. It thrives in well-drained, acidic soils among granite boulders and alongside other alpine survivors like diapensia and mountain sandwort.

seasonality.spring: Emerges slowly as snow melts, with fresh kidney-shaped leaves unfurling from overwintered crowns. Growth is gradual due to harsh alpine conditions and short growing season.
seasonality.summer: Produces its small reddish flower spikes from July through August, the peak identification time. Leaves are at their most succulent and tangy during this period.
seasonality.fall: Develops conspicuous bright red or pink winged fruits that often persist longer than flowers. Leaves may take on reddish tinges before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant and hidden under snow for 6-8 months. Only the underground crown survives the extreme alpine winter conditions.

funFact: Alpine sorrel is one of the few plants that can photosynthesize at temperatures below freezing, allowing it to take advantage of brief sunny moments even when ice crystals form on its leaves!
confusionNotes: The kidney-shaped leaves might remind you of wild ginger, but alpine sorrel's sour taste and high-elevation habitat are dead giveaways. Remember: if you're not above treeline on a mountain peak and it doesn't taste lemony-sour, it's not alpine sorrel!
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this with wood sorrel (Oxalis species) despite the similar common name and sour taste. Alpine sorrel belongs to the buckwheat family, while wood sorrel is in the oxalis family and has three-leaflet clover-like leaves instead of kidney-shaped ones.
compareHints: Alpine sorrel is the only member of its genus Oxyria in New England, making it unique in the region. Within the buckwheat family, it's easily distinguished from relatives like dock and knotweed by its distinctive kidney-shaped leaves and extreme alpine habitat. Most other buckwheat family members have lance-shaped or oval leaves and grow at much lower elevations.
